figure.name: Bill Gates
figure.era: Software monopoly, global philanthropy, and platform wealth (1975-present)
figure.role: Microsoft cofounder, software capitalist, billionaire philanthropist, and central figure in debates over monopoly power and private public-good funding.
figure.hook: Gates = software monopoly, antitrust pressure, and billionaire philanthropy.
whyHere: Gates belongs here because modern capitalism is not only factories, railroads, and banks. It is also software platforms, intellectual property, network effects, antitrust law, and foundation power.

He matters because he shows both sides of concentrated wealth: Microsoft became a defining private technology empire, while Gates later used private philanthropy to shape global health and education debates.
figure.cleanIdea: A billionaire can fund public-good work and still raise democratic questions about monopoly power, private agenda-setting, and who gets to steer public life. Gates is the bridge from twentieth-century antitrust to twenty-first-century philanthropy and platform wealth.

hallCard.timelineMeaning: Microsoft turns software, operating systems, network effects, antitrust fights, and philanthropy into a modern capitalism hallway.

ideas.title: Software Monopoly
ideas.plainDefinition: Software monopoly means a firm gains durable power over a digital market through operating systems, standards, licensing, defaults, bundling, network effects, or lock-in.
ideas.context: In the Gates path, monopoly is not only owning factories. It is controlling the platform where other software and users have to live.
ideas.whyMatters: Software monopoly matters because modern capitalism can concentrate power through code, interfaces, contracts, and defaults, not only through land or machines. The lesson is that control over a platform can shape the choices available to customers, developers, competitors, and whole industries.

sources.title: DOJ / U.S. v. Microsoft Findings of Fact

ideas.title: Antitrust
ideas.plainDefinition: Antitrust is law and policy aimed at protecting competition by limiting monopoly power, restraints of trade, price-fixing, and anti-competitive conduct.
ideas.context: On this road, antitrust is a democratic/legal counterweight to private market power. It is where capitalism admits that competition may need public rules to stay real.
ideas.whyMatters: Antitrust matters because a market can stop acting like a fair contest when one firm controls the door, the defaults, the infrastructure, or the price. Rockefeller and Gates belong here because Standard Oil and Microsoft both became examples of private power large enough to bring law back into the market story.
ideas.carefulVersion: Antitrust is not anti-business by default. It is about the difference between winning by better work and maintaining power by suppressing competition. The hard cases ask whether success came from merit, exclusion, control over access, predatory behavior, or political influence.

ideas.title: Philanthropy Capital
ideas.plainDefinition: Philanthropy capital is private wealth used to fund public-good work, often through foundations, grants, research programs, and agenda-setting institutions.
ideas.context: In the Gates path, philanthropy is real public-good work and also a democratic-accountability question.
ideas.whyMatters: Philanthropy capital matters because helping people with private wealth does not erase the question of who decides priorities and who answers to the public. This is not a cheap attack on charity; it is the democratic question raised when private fortunes fund public-good work at global scale.
